newsitem.title: USA: Clinton challenges Republicans on defense.
newsitem.headline: Clinton challenges Republicans on defense.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday proposed an austere $265 billion U.S. defence budget for 1998 in defiance of a Republican-controlled Congress that wants $6.8 billion more for the military.

The request for defence spending authority in the fiscal year beginning on Oct. 1 is a key part of Clinton's $1.69 trillion federal budget and includes a portion of a $3.5 billion payment to keep U.S. troops in Bosnia another 18 months.

Despite a drive by Clinton and Congress to slash spending and balance the federal budget early in the 21st century, the defence request is likely to spark a fight with Republicans who worry that post-Cold War defence spending has dropped dangerously.
The $265 billion request compares to defence spending authority of $262 billion in current fiscal 1997.

Defence officials told reporters they expected protests over the size of the Bosnia request, $1.5 billion in the budget plus an additional $2 billion to be asked for separately, though Congress seldom rejects money for troops already committed abroad.

Congress approved U.S. troops for the NATO peacekeeping operation in Bosnia for one year, ending last month. But Clinton and allied leaders decided to keep troops there 18 months more to give peace a better chance to last.
Legislators including Sen. Dan Coats, an Indiana Republican, criticised Clinton for making the commitment without Congress's advance approval but Coats predicted Congress would go along.

The Republican-controlled Congress has added billions of dollars to each of Clinton's defence requests, accusing Clinton of cuts jeopardising military readiness, and is likely to add money again this year.
Congress had already allotted $272 billion for defence for next year in the budget resolution it approved last year, $6.8 billion more than Clinton's new request.
Defence spending authority includes additional money for projects that will continue over several years.
The defence authority request for 1998 is over $13 billion higher that the less-inclusive "military authority" figure contained in the summary budget tables.
Defence outlays reflect only the money spent in a particular year and that figure can be higher or lower than authority, depending on what items that money is being spent on.
Clinton's proposed fiscal 1998 outlays total $259 billion compared to $267 billion in 1997.
Clinton's new defence request includes:

-- $3.5 billion for anti-missile defences that would continue only to develop a U.S. missile defence that could be built by 2003 rather that commit to the construction as congressional Republicans want. But in a concession to the legislators, it would speed up delivery of advanced battlefield anti-missiles like those used in the Gulf War.
-- $3 billion for three Aegis destroyers built by Bath Iron Works and Ingalls Shipbuilding.
-- $3 billion for development of a new attack submarine by General Dynamics Electric Boat Division and the Newport News Shipbuilding and Drydock Co.
-- $2.5 billion for 20 advanced Navy F/A-18E/F fighter-bombers built by McDonnell Douglas Corp.
-- $2.4 billion for nine more C-17 combat transport planes built by McDonnell Douglas.
-- $2.2 billion for developmnent of a new Air Force F-22 radar-evading stealth fighter plane by Lockheed Martin and Boeing.
-- A 2.8 percent military pay raise.
